column4: The source section's field opens with rain from above; here water is poured abundantly before the ground is split and planted, making rain the first condition of growth.
The source section explicitly glosses its root ف ل ح through ploughing and splitting earth; this verse names the ground being split, the soil-work behind the image.
The source section's ploughing and ز ك و as crop growth become concrete in the grain that sprouts from the opened earth.
The source section sets fertile land against sand that yields nothing; this verse contrasts good soil whose growth comes by its Lord's leave with foul soil yielding only scant growth.
The source section turns sky and earth into a watered field; this hillside garden receives a downpour and gives double yield, showing what the same rain can nourish in receptive ground.
The source section contrasts growing soil with what produces nothing; here rain strips the thin soil from a stone and leaves it bare, a direct boundary to the fruitful garden in 2:265.
The source section says the nafs grows like a field; this verse makes the human being itself a plant grown from earth, joining moral growth to cultivation.
The source section follows ploughing with seed growth; this verse describes God splitting grain and seed-stones and bringing living from dead, the hidden opening that begins a crop.
The source section makes rain and plant one field image; this verse sends water down and grows grain, dates, grapes, olives, and pomegranates from it.
The source section's watered field is pictured flourishing and then failing: rain mingles with earth's growth until it is adorned, then a command leaves it cut down as though it had not flourished.
The source section calls the sky rain and plant in its dictionary account; here water comes from the sky and supports drink, trees, and pasture.
The source section describes a watered, spreading crop; this verse explicitly says water grows grain, olives, palms, and grapes.
The source section's dry, unproductive land has its reversal here: dead earth stirs, swells, and grows every beautiful kind, alongside human formation from earth.
The source section sets flourishing soil against sand that yields nothing; here rain-fed vegetation turns to dry fragments scattered by wind, showing growth's passing.
The source section joins rain to crop growth; this verse traces water through the earth to varied crops, then their yellowing and reduction to debris.
The source section treats cultivation as the work behind أَفْلَحَ; this verse asks the reader to look at what people plough, opening a direct agricultural counterpart.
The source section reads ز ك و as the crop's growing; this verse asks who makes the sown crop grow, locating growth with God.
The source section's barren sand and buried seed mark growth's opposite; this verse says a crop could instead be made into dry debris.
The source section asks what becomes fit to grow; this continuation records the cultivators' loss after the crop is ruined, the human consequence of failed yield.
The source section contrasts fertile growth with nothing yielding; this continuation names deprivation after the crop's loss.
The source section turns the sky above and earth below into a field-house; this verse joins earth as a resting place, sky as a canopy, rain, and fruit as provision.
The source section's field yields growth from earth; this verse tells people to give from good things earned and grown from the earth, distinguishing sound produce from what one would reject.
The source section calls Thamud a people of cultivated land; Salih reminds them that God brought them from earth and settled them in it, giving the land a human-growing sense.
The source section identifies Thamud with fields and palms; this adjacent verse names their crops and palms with tender fruit, specifying the cultivated abundance around them.
The source section links cloud, rain, and a green carpet of plants; this verse sends a laden wind-driven cloud to dead land and revives earth with it.
The source section's root ز ك و names growth and blessing; this verse makes rain revive dead earth a sign for those who listen.
The source section pictures sky-water spreading life over earth; here rain makes the earth green, so the field's change is visible.
The source section says the dwelling's roof and floor become a field; this verse describes earth as a bed, paths through it, and rain bringing out varied plants.
The source section's field is watered to produce growth; this verse brings water to barren land and grows crops for people and their livestock.
The source section follows water opening through soil into growth; this verse names blessed rain growing gardens and harvest grain.
The source section links crop growth to provision; this verse says the rain-grown yield is sustenance for servants and revives a dead town.
The source section's crop roots into soil and multiplies; this verse's good tree has a firm root and a high branch, making rootedness the condition for growth.
The source section describes growth that continues through blessing; this tree gives fruit at every season by its Lord's permission.
The source section opposes rooted growth to what is buried and cannot sprout; this bad tree is uprooted and has no stability.
The source section contrasts good land with land that scarcely yields; here adjoining plots receive the same water yet differ in their produce.
The source section's crop-growth gloss for ز ك و meets this image of one grain producing seven ears and multiplied harvest, making growth a figure for increase.
The source section evokes a watered home becoming a field; this garden has palms, vines, and streams, yet a fiery whirlwind burns it, the loss of cultivated growth.
The source section's field depends on what nourishes it; this verse's cold wind strikes a people's crop and destroys it, showing the reverse of rain-fed growth.
The source section contrasts cultivated yield with barren ground; this garden is ruined until its owner turns his hands over what he spent and sees it collapsed.
The source section presents land whose plants sustain a people; Sheba's two gardens furnish food and a call to gratitude from the Lord.
The source section names sand that grows nothing; after the people turn away, their gardens are replaced by bitter, sparse growth.
The source section's irrigated earth spreads into growth; this verse says barren ground stirs and swells when water reaches it.
The source section's field image depends on earth made productive; this verse spreads earth and grows things in measured balance.
The source section describes opened watercourses and a field's water share; this verse sends fertilizing winds and water down from the sky to drink.
The source section's cloud and rain nourish the field; this verse says rain revives a dead town and waters animals and people.
The source section shows land becoming a planted field; this verse asks how many noble pairs of growth have been brought forth from earth.
The source section turns the sky's water into a cultivated ground; this verse asks who grows beautiful gardens by rain and makes their rivers flow.
The source section names cloud, rain, and plant as one field system; this verse follows winds lifting clouds until rain emerges from them.
The source section makes soil's growth visible; this verse directs the reader to the signs of mercy in how God revives earth after its death.
The source section's field is earth watered from above; this verse explicitly connects rain with growing every noble kind of plant.
The source section traces nourishment from cloud to ground; this verse drives a cloud to dead land and revives earth with rain.
The source section's ground is split and made to yield; this verse calls dead earth a sign and says grain is brought out of it.
The source section describes soil watered into growth; this verse places date and grape gardens and springs in that revived land.
The source section asks what the field produces; this verse points to fruit for people to eat, a provision they did not make grow by their own hands.
The source section describes the earth spread as a field; this verse pairs that spread with mountains and every beautiful kind of growth.
The source section names palms among the people of Thamud; this verse shows tall palms with clustered fruit as a sign of provision.
The source section treats earth as a field laid open for growth; this verse says earth is set out for living creatures.
The source section's cultivated field yields fruit; this verse names fruit and date palms among the earth's provision.
The source section depicts growing crops; this verse names grain with husk and fragrant plants as earth's yield.
The source section says the self is grown like a plant and links the Lord to nurture; this verse joins rain with gardens and rivers as gifts.
The source section's soil is opened to water and growth; this verse names water and pasture brought from the spread earth.
The source section's field is a place of spreading plant life; this verse says God brings out pasture from earth.
The source section contrasts flourishing soil with barren sand; the pasture is then made dry, dark stubble, the field's reverse.
The source section glosses ز ك و as a crop's growth and links it to cleansing the self; this verse joins success with تزكى, preserving both moral purification and the growth sense.
The source section explicitly reads تزكى through the root's growth and blessing; this verse places that growth-word beside gardens with rivers as the reward.
The source section glosses أَفْلَحَ through ف ل ح, the farmer who splits earth; this verse uses the same verb for believers' success, letting the field-work sense illuminate flourishing.
The source section says دَسَّىٰهَا evokes pressing into earth and opposes ز ك و growth; this verse's question about burying a girl in dust gives the literal scene and its moral reversal.
The source section defines the dictionary form الفجرة as a place where water opens; this verse's demanded spring bursting from earth is a direct water-opening scene.
The source section's root ف ج ر names the place water opens; this verse has earth opening into springs, an exact landscape counterpart.
The source section glosses س ق ي as a land's allotted share of drinking water; this verse gives the she-camel and people separate, appointed drinking turns.
The source section treats سُقْيَا as the camel's water share; this verse explicitly orders that the water be divided between them.
The source section connects ع ق ر with cutting the growing point of a palm; here the same act-root names the killing of the she-camel whose water was shared.
The source section sets fruitful palms against barren land; after the camel is killed, the people become like dry palm stumps or gathered stubble.
The source section's dictionary gloss for ف ج ر is water opening in earth; here striking stone makes twelve springs gush, with water assigned to each group.
The source section uses rain and plant-growth to turn earth into a field; this sign passage links clouds, rain, rivers, and revived earth.
The source section's cultivated land yields crops and fruit; this verse names gardens, dates, vines, harvest, and the right owed from its produce.
The source section ends its field account with the Thamud and the she-camel; this verse presents that camel as God's sign to the same people.
The source section calls Thamud a people of the field; this continuation places them in the land's plains and describes their homes and settled use of it.
The source section links ع ق ر to cutting a palm's growing head; this verse uses the root for the act against Salih's camel, the field's fruitful animal struck down.
The source section glosses س ق ي through a measured drinking share; this verse gives each Israelite group its own known drinking place at the springs.
The source section connects the camel's water share with cultivated land; Salih tells Thamud to let her graze on God's earth and not harm her.
The source section's ع ق ر branch concerns cutting growth; this verse says Thamud hamstrung the camel after the warning about her grazing.
The source section treats earth as the place where growth is spread; this verse describes earth extended with fruits and paired kinds, under day and night.
The source section joins rain and land to provision; this verse names rain, fruit, rivers, and ships among God's provision.
The source section links the soil's growth to provision; this verse says livelihood is placed in earth for people and other creatures.
The source section's field becomes garden through water and cultivation; this verse stages two grape gardens ringed by palms and crops.
The source section describes the crop reaching growth; this continuation says both gardens yield their fruit and a river runs between them.
The source section names waterways in slopes and a land's water share; this verse warns that the garden's water could sink into the earth and become inaccessible.
The source section's soil has a water share; this verse says water is settled in earth but can also be taken away.
The source section describes a home turned into field; this verse grows gardens of palms and grapes with abundant fruit for eating.
The source section links sky-water and land-growth; this verse describes pure water sent from above before the dead-town revival in 25:49.
The source section says Thamud lived amid cultivated land; this verse names their gardens and springs.
The source section describes Thamud's water allotment and the she-camel; this continuation forbids harming her and completes the water-share warning.
The source section's ع ق ر dictionary branch is cutting a palm's growth point; this verse says they hamstrung the camel and regretted it.
The source section joins Thamud's act against the camel to the Lord's response; this continuation supplies the punishment that follows their slaughter.
The source section depicts rain as the field's nourishment; this verse describes people's despair before rain arrives, completing the cloud scene in 30:48.
The source section describes rain reaching soil and growth; this verse says water descends by measure and spreads life through a dead town.
The source section's root ط ح و describes plant spread over earth's face; this verse describes earth laid out as a bed, the surface on which that carpet lies.
The source section's date-palm dictionary branch concerns cutting its crown; this verse likens the ruined people to uprooted palm trunks.
The source section links the she-camel's killing to the field's destruction; this continuation asks how the warning and punishment came after the act.
The source section joins sky, rain, and a growing field; this verse promises abundant rain, followed immediately by gardens and rivers in 71:12.
The source section describes earth's surface as spread for plant life; this verse says earth was spread out, preparing the water and pasture named in 79:31.
The source section uses the sky as rain and the ground as a field; this verse calls the sky returning rain, completing the natural condition for the earth's split in 86:12.
The source section's land is opened to water and growth; this verse names earth with a split, alongside the rain-bearing sky in 86:11.
The source section's image centers on land cultivated for growth; this verse begins a garden story with owners who expect its harvest.

The source section contrasts growth with land that yields nothing; the garden becomes كَالصَّرِيمِ, which can mean darkened or reaped, so the cut-field reading recalls the image but remains uncertain.
The source section traces what a field can yield or lose; after seeing the ruined garden, its owners recognize they were deprived.
The source section invokes 16:59's burial of a girl in soil; this preceding verse gives the disgrace and concealment that lead into that burial, though it does not itself describe earth or growth.

The source section explicitly connects water opening through rock to the field and to a heart made hard; this verse says rivers burst from some stones, giving the image its precise hard-surface reversal.

The source section opposes cultivated growth to burying and barren yield; this verse names a person who corrupts the land and destroys both harvest and offspring, showing growth being actively undone.
The source section sets fruitful earth against ground that grows nothing; Abraham names a valley without cultivation and asks God to provide fruit there, making provision answer the barren landscape.
The source section identifies the root ز ك و with growth arising from God's blessing; this verse contrasts increase sought through usury with zakah given for God's sake and multiplied by Him.

The source section's dictionary form عَقَرْت النخلة describes cutting a palm's growing crown; this verse speaks of cutting palm trees or leaving them standing, giving that destructive agricultural act a Qur'anic scene.
The source section recalls burying a girl in earth as the opposite of growth; this verse's الموءودة is the buried-alive girl, a repeated Qur'anic formulation of that scene.

The source section turns crop growth into a way to read moral increase; this verse says God erases usury and makes charitable giving grow, carrying the field's growth-versus-loss contrast into giving.
The source section names river-cut earth and water channels on slopes; this verse's valleys carry water in measured quantities, a specific picture of channels directing water through land.
The source section defines ف ج ر through water opening; this verse asks for a garden of dates and grapes with rivers gushing through it, joining the field and opened watercourse.
The source section pictures water opening and moving through cultivated land; following the gardens in 27:60, this verse contributes fixed earth, rivers, and barriers between waters.
The source section links the she-camel's water share to the Thamud's test; this verse calls the camel a trial, completed by the water division in 54:28.
The source section evokes the buried girl in 16:59; after this verse's buried-alive girl, this ayah asks what sin she was killed for, stating the moral wrong in that parallel.
